stories.headline: Golden Police Officer Shot at Circle K Gas Station; Suspect Killed
stories.summary:
A Golden police officer was shot early Saturday morning after a suspect opened fire at a Circle K gas station, according to Denver7. The officer sustained a non-life-threatening injury and is expected to survive. The suspect was killed during the incident.

Details surrounding the circumstances that led to the shooting were not immediately available. Golden police have not yet released the identities of the officer or the suspect involved.

The shooting adds to a string of violent incidents involving law enforcement across the Denver metro area this summer. Investigators are continuing to examine the events leading up to the confrontation.

stories.headline: Dangerous Heat and Smoky Skies to Grip Colorado Through Weekend; Relief Expected Midweek
stories.summary:
A ridge of high pressure building over Colorado is expected to push afternoon temperatures into the upper 90s to around 105 degrees across the plains this weekend, potentially making it Denver's hottest stretch of the summer. A Heat Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Saturday through 8 p.m. Sunday across the Denver metro area. Denver could record its sixth and seventh triple-digit days of the year — a remarkable figure given the city typically averages only one such day annually.

Thick smoke drifting in from wildfires burning in the Pacific Northwest is blanketing much of Colorado, prompting Air Quality Health Advisories through the weekend. Residents with respiratory conditions or asthma are advised to limit time outdoors. Overnight lows will offer little relief, only dipping into the upper 60s near 70 degrees.

Fire danger remains elevated statewide amid the hot, dry conditions. Temperatures are expected to stay in the upper 90s along the Interstate 25 corridor through Monday and Tuesday before monsoon moisture returns mid-week, bringing cloud cover and storm chances that should ease the heat.

stories.headline: Update: Elk Fire Nearly Doubles in Size, Containment Drops to 34% as Lake City Remains on Pre-Evacuation Warning
stories.summary:
The Elk Fire burning outside Lake City in Hinsdale County has grown to 6,213 acres — nearly doubling in size over two days — while containment dropped from 42% to 34%, fire officials reported Saturday. Forty-two structures in the San Juan Springs subdivision north of Lake City are now under mandatory evacuation orders. The entire town of Lake City, home to approximately 400 residents, remains on a pre-evacuation warning.

Fire managers have doubled the number of personnel on scene to 104, with more crews on the way. Crews are focusing on protecting homes and structures by laying hoses, placing water tanks, and installing other water-handling equipment. Officials are also developing contingency plans in the event the fire jumps Colorado 149 to the east.

Two western divisions of the fire currently have no firefighters assigned to them, as the highest priority remains protecting homes and structures to the south and southeast. A new incident management team is scheduled to rotate in and take command Sunday morning. Updated evacuation information is available through Hinsdale County emergency management.

stories.headline: Indian Creek Fire Forces Mandatory Evacuations in Jackson County
stories.summary:
The Indian Creek Fire has prompted mandatory evacuations in Jackson County, adding to a growing list of active wildfires threatening Colorado communities during an extreme heat and drought period. Specific acreage and containment figures for the fire were not immediately available, but evacuation orders signal the blaze has grown to a level that threatens nearby structures and residents.

Jackson County is a sparsely populated area in north-central Colorado, west of Rocky Mountain National Park. Residents in affected areas have been ordered to leave immediately as firefighting resources across the state remain stretched due to multiple simultaneous fire incidents.

The Indian Creek Fire is among several active wildfires burning in Colorado amid dangerous heat, low humidity, and dry conditions forecast to persist through the weekend. Officials urge the public to avoid activities that could spark additional fires.

stories.headline: Republican Governor Candidate Victor Marx's Extraordinary Backstory Becomes Liability on Campaign Trail
stories.summary:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, is facing mounting scrutiny over the dramatic personal stories that once powered his Christian nonprofit ministry — including claims that his stepfather forced him to behead a cat as a child and later fatally shoot a man. Those narratives, which Marx detailed in two books and a documentary, helped build a multimillion-dollar fundraising operation but are now drawing pointed questions from media and political opponents as Marx seeks statewide office in a state where more than half of residents do not identify as religious.

Marx has grown frustrated with the line of questioning, writing on social media after a contentious interview with British commentator Piers Morgan that he had wanted to discuss his campaign platform but found himself relitigating "old narratives and repeated accusations that have already been addressed." Former Republican Congressman and state party chair Ken Buck noted that unlike candidates with legislative records, Marx's personal backstory is the primary basis for voters to evaluate him.

Marx won the GOP gubernatorial nomination as a political newcomer, partly by citing his personal achievements and life experiences as qualifications for the office. He now faces the challenge of shifting focus to policy while the stories that defined his nonprofit career continue to dominate press coverage. The general election is scheduled for November.

stories.headline: Denver Economist Tatiana Bailey Breaks Down Slowing GDP Growth and What It Means for Colorado Consumers
stories.summary:
The first estimate of U.S. gross domestic product for the second quarter of 2026 showed annualized growth of 1.5% — a slowdown in economic activity, though still positive. Denver-based economist Tatiana Bailey, writing in the Denver Gazette, attributed the soft reading largely to declines in government spending and a rise in imports, which subtract from GDP calculations. Consumer spending and private fixed investment remained the largest contributors to growth.

Bailey highlighted concern over the national savings rate, which fell to 2.7% in June, well below the historical average of roughly 8%. A serious credit card delinquency rate — defined as 90-plus days past due — has climbed to 7.1%, suggesting financial stress is spreading among lower- and middle-income households even as higher-income consumers continue spending.

On a more positive note, the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index rose to 54.4 after hitting a near-record low of 49.5 in June, as oil prices eased and inflation moderated. Year-over-year inflation slowed from 4.2% to 3.5% in June, with core inflation holding steady at 2.6%. Bailey cautioned that persistently higher prices remain a drag on consumer confidence across all income levels.

stories.headline: Ultra Lounge East Owner to Surrender Liquor and Cabaret Licenses Following Mass Shooting
stories.summary:
The owner of Ultra Lounge East, a Denver-area nightclub, has agreed to surrender both its liquor license and cabaret license in the wake of a mass shooting connected to the establishment. The license surrender marks a significant step in the regulatory response to the shooting, which prompted investigations by local authorities and licensing boards.

Details of the shooting — including the number of victims and when it occurred — were not elaborated upon in available reporting, but the decision to relinquish licenses indicates that regulators found the venue to have failed to maintain a safe environment. License surrenders of this type are typically the result of negotiations between the owner and licensing authorities to avoid a formal revocation proceeding.

The closure of Ultra Lounge East removes a venue that had become associated with violent crime from operation. Regulators and public safety officials have increasingly used licensing authority as a tool to address establishments linked to repeat violent incidents across the Denver metro area.

stories.headline: Mi Pueblo Market to Open Largest Location at Former Westminster Walmart Site
stories.summary:
Mi Pueblo Market, a grocery chain serving Latino communities, is set to open its largest location at the site of a former Walmart in Westminster. The announcement represents a significant retail development for the Westminster area, filling a major commercial vacancy with a grocery store oriented toward the region's growing Hispanic population.

Specific square footage and an opening date were not detailed in available reporting, but the former Walmart footprint typically encompasses well over 100,000 square feet, suggesting Mi Pueblo's Westminster store would be a substantial expansion for the chain. The site's conversion from a big-box retail anchor to a specialty grocer reflects broader trends in repurposing vacant large-format retail properties.

Mi Pueblo has established a presence in the Denver metro area serving communities where access to Latin American food products and culturally familiar grocery options has historically been limited. The Westminster location is expected to draw shoppers from across the northern metro.

stories.headline: Native Roots Closes Denver Cannabis Grow Facility, Lays Off 141 Employees Following Dispensary Sale
stories.summary:
Native Roots, one of Colorado's largest cannabis retailers, has shut down a Denver grow facility and laid off 141 employees following the sale of its dispensary operations. The layoffs represent one of the larger workforce reductions in the Colorado cannabis industry in recent memory, underscoring continued consolidation and financial pressure in the sector.

The facility closure follows a period of significant disruption in the state's cannabis market, as falling wholesale prices, high taxes, and increasing competition from other states have squeezed operators of all sizes. Native Roots had been among the most prominent multi-location dispensary brands in Colorado since the early days of legal cannabis.

The sale of the dispensary business and subsequent grow closure signals a major restructuring for the company. The affected workers will need to seek employment in a cannabis labor market that has seen widespread contraction across Colorado over the past two years.

stories.headline: Broncos Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph Commands Training Camp as Sean Payton Attends Hall of Fame Ceremony
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph led Saturday's training camp scrimmage in head coach Sean Payton's absence, with Payton traveling to present Drew Brees at the Pro Football Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Canton, Ohio. Joseph, who narrowly missed landing a head coaching job this past offseason despite multiple interviews, directed a Broncos defense that set franchise records with 63 sacks in 2024 and then surpassed it with 68 last season.

Denver Post columnist Nick Renck argued that Joseph is positioned to lead the NFL's top-ranked defense this season, with cornerstones Pat Surtain II, Zach Allen, and Ja'Quan McMillian all returning. Cornerback Riley Moss praised Joseph's player-development philosophy, calling it a "developmental program" where players improve regardless of experience level. The Broncos finished 14-3 last season, with the defense widely credited as the backbone of the team's success.

Joseph's continued presence in Denver comes despite reported interest from multiple franchises seeking a head coach this past offseason. His ability to deliver another dominant defensive season could strengthen both his career prospects and the Broncos' chances in a competitive AFC West. Training camp continues at Dove Valley.

stories.headline: Nuggets' Peyton Watson Saga Drags On as Denver Remains Stuck in Luxury Tax Purgatory
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets remain at an impasse with restricted free agent Peyton Watson, whose agent Rich Paul has been seeking a contract worth approximately $25 million annually. Watson, 23, broke out last season with a 14.6 points-per-game average over 54 games before hamstring injuries cut his year short, but the Nuggets — the lone NBA team in the second apron of the luxury tax — face severe financial constraints on what they can offer.

Denver Gazette columnist Mark Kiszla attributed the team's current salary cap predicament to large contracts handed out to Michael Porter Jr., Aaron Gordon, Christian Braun, and Jamal Murray in recent seasons. The Nuggets' reluctance to meet Watson's asking price has drawn reported interest from the Clippers, Hawks, Bucks, and Cavaliers in potential sign-and-trade scenarios, though the financial dynamics make it unlikely Denver would receive full value in return.

Underlying the Watson situation is broader concern about the franchise's trajectory. The Nuggets have not made a significant roster move this offseason despite being viewed as a championship contender in decline, and anxiety is growing among fans and analysts that superstar Nikola Jokic could explore free agency in 2027 if the organization fails to surround him with a competitive roster. The Nuggets also signed Lonnie Walker IV to a one-year, $3.3 million deal, a modest addition that has done little to quell concerns.

stories.headline: Air Force Football Opens Practice; New Academy Superintendent Gifts Flight Helmet to Deion Sanders
stories.summary:
Air Force Academy football practice opened Saturday with a dramatic touch, as former Falcon fullback Nate Walker piloted an F-16 that made multiple low passes over the practice fields in Colorado Springs. The flyby occurred as Colorado's football team was departing the facility, having used it earlier in the week as part of a training stretch at Fountain-Fort Carson High School. The two teams did not practice together, as NCAA policy prohibits it.

Newly installed Air Force Superintendent Lt. Gen. Paul D. Moga — sworn into the role Friday — presented Colorado head coach Deion Sanders with a custom flight helmet as a goodwill gift from the academy. The exchange highlighted the collegial relationship between the two programs, which share the same state and compete in the same conference.

On the field, Air Force coach Troy Calhoun is working senior Kemper Hodges at both quarterback and fullback, a rare dual role the 6-foot, 245-pound player has experience in from previous seasons. Hodges completed 6 of 14 passes for 74 yards and rushed 49 times for 207 yards and three touchdowns during the 2025 season. Several sophomores are in contention for starting spots in the secondary as fall camp competition heats up.

topStory.headline: Hunter Biden Says Father's Cancer Has Spread to Bones, Calls Condition 'Painful' and 'Debilitating'
topStory.summary:
Hunter Biden disclosed in a televised interview Friday that his father, former President Joe Biden, is experiencing a worsening cancer condition, with the disease having metastasized beyond his bones. Speaking on BBC Newsnight with host Paddy O'Connell, Hunter Biden grew emotional as he described his father's illness as "very painful" and "very debilitating," adding: "I wish he would complain more, because it's not good."

Joe Biden, 83, was diagnosed in May 2025 with an aggressive form of prostate cancer, graded at a Gleason score of 9, placing him in Grade Group 5, the most severe category. His office reported in October 2025 that he had completed a round of radiation therapy and hormone treatment, though it remained unclear whether additional care would be required. Former first lady Jill Biden previously told NBC News that her husband would "live with cancer till the rest of his life" given the extent to which the disease had spread.

Hunter Biden also addressed his father's widely scrutinized performance at the June 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump, saying he watched it alone at his California home and was immediately alarmed. "I could tell as soon as my father came out that something was wrong," he said, describing an unusual "hundred-yard stare" he had never seen before. He suggested the underlying cancer, diagnosed months later, may have been a contributing factor to the performance that ultimately prompted Joe Biden to withdraw from the 2024 presidential race.

In the same interview, Hunter Biden reflected on the broad presidential pardon his father granted him before leaving office in January 2025, which covered potential federal offenses between January 2014 and December 2024. He called the pardon "not fair" but acknowledged his gratitude, saying his father "chose me over his legacy." Hunter Biden had been facing federal gun charges and had previously pleaded guilty to tax evasion charges before the pardon was issued.

The interview arrives as Joe Biden remains publicly active despite his condition, with a memoir titled "Promise Me, America" scheduled for release after the midterm elections. Former first lady Jill Biden has said the cancer diagnosis was a shock to the family, noting that routine PSA screenings are not typically recommended for men over 70 under American Urological Association guidelines, which she offered as a partial explanation for why the cancer was not detected during his time in the White House.
